observations.note: The first reading asks how real earthly duties and goods remain subordinate to God; Jerome’s unknowing Cyrus, Chrysostom’s bounded tribute, Aquinas’s explicitly mystical divine-image application and Augustine’s worldwide new song contribute different reasoning. The second asks how the person becomes willing and able to serve; Aquinas’s inward divine action and Chrysostom’s costly faith, love and hope carry the argument, with Jerome’s gifted teacher and Bede’s prior saving gift contributing further reasoning. These are distinguishable complementary interpretations, not two versions of one application. Each engages all ten ritual positions and both Communion alternatives, and differentiates literal, allegorical, moral and anagogical senses.

observations.note: Consequential-difficulty test passed. The study explains why the ignorance clause controls that distinction and why useful political action is not proof of conversion. Its use of Jerome’s concluding application to the gifted ecclesial teacher follows the actual source argument. The study therefore neither abolishes civil duties nor turns Caesar’s claim into an unlimited claim on the person.

observations.note: Consequential-difficulty test passed. The checked Latin rejects both autonomous saving choice and the elimination of free choice; divine movement acts inwardly in the will. It also rejects assigning the beginning of willing to the person independently and only completion to God, or treating help as payment for merit before grace. The study teaches these successive distinctions and connects them intelligibly to the Collect and to received light. Philippians 2:12–13 is explicitly identified as context, not the appointed acclamation.

observations.note: The PL print image confirms Bede’s sequence: the servant’s form and blood shed for the world, followed by his gloss of for many as those willing to believe. lanes.title: Receiving the world without worshipping its powers
The received gift becomes willing service

summary: The independently rebuilt 23-page study passes the cold review: two distinct, coherent whole-formulary interpretations develop substantive reasoning from multiple Fathers and saints, each with its own four senses, and the complete text and all physical pages were inspected. Consequential checks at Jerome In Isaiam XII on Isaiah 45:1–7, Chrysostom Matthew LXX §§1–2, Aquinas Philippians 2.3, and Bede In Marci III, PL 92 col.236B confirm the study’s distinctions among Cyrus and Christ, civil obligation and divine allegiance, grace and willing action, and ransom and believing reception; no blocking or advisory defect was found.
